B: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
A: Yes, hi. I can hear you fine. I'm Usman.
B: Callum. Nice to meet you, mate.
A: Nice to meet you too. Er, where are you calling from?
B: Long Eaton. It's between Nottingham and Derby, sort of in the middle. You?
A: Ilford, in East London.
B: Nice. I've only really been to London for a couple of gigs, to be honest. In and out on the train. So, er, what do you do?
A: I'm an accountant. I do audit, mostly manufacturing and logistics companies. It's quite boring to explain, I think.
B: Nah, go on. What does that actually involve, day to day?
A: Er, so a company produces its accounts, and we check they are right. We look at the numbers, test the stock, check the contracts. If something doesn't add up, we ask questions. Some clients like that, some don't. At the moment it's quiet, but January to March is very busy. Long hours.
B: Right. So you're the one who comes in and says "that doesn't look right."
A: Yes, sort of. Politely. What about you?
B: I'm a joiner. I work for a small firm in Beeston doing heritage stuff. Sash windows, doors, staircases, a lot of old houses, some listed buildings. Half the time I'm in the workshop and half the time I'm out fitting. At the minute we're doing a Georgian townhouse in Southwell, all the windows. Some of the original frames are about two hundred years old, so you're trying to save as much of the timber as you can rather than just ripping it out.
A: Two hundred years. That's impressive. Is that difficult?
B: It can be. You've got to be patient with it. You cut out the rotten bit and splice new wood in, and it's got to match, you know what I mean? You don't want it looking like a patch.
A: Yes. I can imagine. So it's like an audit for windows.
B: Ha, yeah, actually, that's not bad. You check what's wrong and you don't cut corners.
A: Exactly.
B: Is that a cricket trophy on your shelf there?
A: Ah, yes. It's small. We play on Sundays in Valentines Park, tape-ball and softball. We won a little tournament last summer.
B: Are you a batter or a bowler?
A: Bowler. Medium pace. I'm not fast anymore.
B: I don't know much about cricket, if I'm honest. My dad's more football, Derby County. I'll go to the odd game with him.
A: I'm the opposite. I know the football table because people talk about it at work, but cricket is the one I really follow. Pakistan. I stay up until three in the morning sometimes for matches.
B: Three in the morning. And then work the next day?
A: Yes. It's not a good idea. But when it's a close game, you can't sleep anyway.
B: Fair enough. Is that where you're from originally, Pakistan?
A: Yes, Lahore. I came here for my master's when I was twenty-two and stayed. Eight years now.
B: I've heard Lahore's got some amazing old buildings. I'm into that sort of thing, old architecture. I'd like to go one day.
A: Yes, the old city is very beautiful. The Badshahi Mosque, the fort. And the food is the best part, honestly.
B: Oh, go on then, what should I eat?
A: Er, karahi. Chicken karahi. I make it most Fridays, actually, but my mum's is better.
